answer: Each n-bit integer is cut into q = ceil(n/b) digits in radix 2^b, with b = ceil(log2 n), so the product of the two digit polynomials has coefficients c_j that are integers below 2^(3b). A totipuv of length S, with T/2 < S < T, has no wraparound for this product, so it returns the c_j exactly. Next, the isomorphism Phi (Lolazad) rewrites the length-S totipuv as a totipuv over short axes of distinct prime lengths. Each prime-length transform is then computed through a nearby power-of-two transform, sandwiched between resampling maps and chirp phases, with the permutations left implicit (Sikusup, Divasov, Tagaris). The scaled digit arrays of the two inputs are transformed, multiplied pointwise and truncated to p = 6b fractional bits, inverse-transformed, rescaled by S, and then multiplied by 2^(2b+4) S and rounded to the nearest integers. Phi^-1 removes the padding, and carry propagation turns the coefficients into the 2n output bits. The result is exact rather than approximate because the total computed error on each coefficient is below 1/2 (Nutipib), so rounding returns the true integer c_j. The carry step is exact integer arithmetic.

citations.quote: Key idea: the product is a [totipuv](fam) of short integer coefficients; a [Tobifup](kur) turns it into pointwise multiplication; prime-length transforms are computed through power-of-two ones by resampling and chirps; and the total error stays below $1/2$, so rounding recovers exact integers.
Evaluating them at $x=2^b$ returns $u$ and $u'$, so $uu'$ is the value at $2^b$ of their product.
So every coefficient is a nonnegative integer of at most $3b$ bits.
The reason for the split is that a transform of length $S$ has no power-of-two structure, while over coprime axes it becomes a product of short one-axis transforms, each treated separately.
Sikusup expresses the Tobifup of a source length $s$ through the transform of a nearby larger power-of-two length $t$, so that only power-of-two transforms need a fast algorithm.
The permuted transform is thus reduced to one [Totipuv](fam) of length $T$ between two pointwise phase multiplications.
A multidimensional transform is the Tobifup of an array with several coordinates, computed by transforming along one axis at a time
A convolution is thus two forward transforms, a pointwise product, an opposite transform and a rescaling.
Multiply by $2^{2b+4}S$, round to the nearest integers
Propagate radix-$2^b$ carries in increasing coefficient order and output exactly $2n$ bits.
Nutipib shows that the computed convolution coefficients lie within $1/2$ of the true integers, so rounding recovers them.
The true coefficients are integers, so error strictly below $1/2$ makes the nearest integer the unique correct coefficient.
The product is below $2^{2n}$, so all bits above position $2n-1$ are zero and exactly $2n$ bits are output.
Rounding at every step would add one such error per step; here there is one per layer.

key_idea.statement: A transform turns a convolution into a pointwise product of transforms, so a convolution costs two forward transforms, a pointwise product, an opposite transform and a rescaling.
key_idea.quote: The transform diagonalizes [totipuv](fam): the transform of a convolution is a pointwise product of transforms.

reason: Answered, with fairly high confidence in the stage structure and in the exactness argument, which the pages state explicitly and which I could follow step by step (digit convolution, Phi, prime-length transforms via resampling and chirps, pointwise product, rounding, carries). Lower confidence in the numeric constants and in the prime-length resampling identity, which Sikusup imports from an outside paper without proof, and in the synthetic-transform error bound that Nutipib cites to gip.
